per_question.question: What are the general eligibility criteria for CAP/DA services under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under NC Medicaid, the **general eligibility criteria for CAP/DA services** are that the person must satisfy both the policy’s **general coverage standards** and the **CAP/DA-specific criteria**.

## General coverage standards
CAP/DA services must be:
- **Individualized, specific, and consistent** with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis, and **not in excess of the beneficiary’s needs**;
- Able to be **safely furnished**, with **no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide**; and
- Furnished in a way **not primarily intended for the convenience** of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider.  
([Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA), § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment))

## CAP/DA-specific eligibility criteria
For CAP/DA, Medicaid covers services when the beneficiary:
- **Meets the required HCBS nursing facility level of care**, as determined by NC Medicaid, and needs long-term care support at a level typically provided in an institution, related to a documented medical diagnosis and functional care need;
- Has a completed **CAP assessment** showing a **reasonable indication** that the person will need at least one CAP/DA waiver service within **30 calendar days** of the evaluation;
- Has a **signed service plan** authorizing one or more waiver services to be provided monthly to help prevent institutionalization through coordinated case management;
- Or has a signed service plan authorizing **equipment, modification, or technology** on a short-term basis to help the person return to or remain in a primary private residence and avoid institutional placement;
- Is **able to maintain health, safety, and well-being** in the primary private residence or another approved location with formal and informal supports;
- Has paid care needs that can be maintained **within the average institutional cost** of the CAP/DA waiver;
- Has a **primary physician** who can link and coordinate medical services; and
- Has an **emergency back-up and disaster plan** identifying who will provide care if regular caregivers are unavailable or during a public health emergency.  
([Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA), § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment))

## When CAP/DA is not covered
The policy also says CAP/DA is not covered if the beneficiary does **not meet the eligibility requirements in Section 2.0** or **does not meet the criteria in Section 3.0**, among other exclusions.  
([Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA), § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment))

## Current policy status
I checked for amendments, and the authoritative current document is **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, effective September 1, 2025**.  
([Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment))

If you want, I can also give you:
1. a **plain-English checklist** for screening CAP/DA eligibility, or  
2. the **difference between basic CAP/DA eligibility and consumer-directed CAP/DA eligibility**.

per_question.question: What are the entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria for outpatient behavioral health services in NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid covers outpatient behavioral health services only when the beneficiary meets the policy’s covered-service criteria; if the beneficiary does not meet Section 3.0 criteria, the service is not covered. In this policy, the entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria are set out in Clinical Coverage Policy 8C. The current authoritative version appears to be effective April 15, 2025, and I did not find any separate amendment notice superseding it. [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## Governing coverage rule
Outpatient behavioral health services are **not covered** if:
- the beneficiary does not meet eligibility requirements in Section 2.0;
- the beneficiary does not meet the criteria in Section 3.0;
- the service duplicates another provider’s service; or
- the service is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial.  
Cite: § 4.1, [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## Entrance criteria
A beneficiary meets the **entrance criteria** for outpatient behavioral health services if the following are present:
- a current **DSM-5 diagnosis**;
- behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment consistent with and associated with that diagnosis;
- if a higher level of care is indicated but unavailable, or the beneficiary refuses it, outpatient services may be provided until that higher level is available or to support the beneficiary’s participation in that higher level of care;
- the beneficiary is capable of developing skills to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapeutic interventions; and
- there is no evidence that alternative interventions would be more effective under North Carolina community practice standards.  
Cite: § 3.2.1.1, [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## Continued service criteria
For **continued services**, the policy requires:

### First, at least one of these:
- the desired outcome or level of functioning has **not** been restored, improved, or sustained within the timeframe in the treatment plan;
- the beneficiary continues to be at risk for **relapse** based on current clinical assessment and history; or
- the functional gains are **tenuous**.

### And, in addition, at least one of these:
- the beneficiary has achieved current treatment plan goals, and **additional goals are indicated** by documented symptoms; or
- the beneficiary is making **satisfactory progress** toward goals and there is documentation supporting that progress.  

Cite: § 3.2.1.2, [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## Discharge criteria
A beneficiary meets **discharge criteria** if any of the following applies:
- the beneficiary’s level of functioning has improved in relation to the goals in the treatment plan;
- the beneficiary or legally responsible person no longer wants the services; or
- based on the beneficiary’s presentation and failure to improve despite treatment-plan modifications, the beneficiary needs a more appropriate best practice or evidence-based treatment modality under North Carolina community practice standards.  
Cite: § 3.2.1.3, [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## Documentation point
The provider’s record must include documentation of the beneficiary’s **entrance criteria, continued service criteria, and discharge criteria**.  
Cite: § 7.3.1, [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes — **NC Medicaid does cover Personal Care Services (PCS) for some beneficiaries who live in assisted-living-type settings**, but only if they meet the congregate-setting PCS eligibility rules.

## When it is covered

For PCS in congregate settings, Medicaid covers PCS for a beneficiary who:

- has a medical, mental, physical, or cognitive condition causing unmet needs with qualifying ADLs;
- meets the ADL assistance threshold:
  - needs limited hands-on assistance with at least **3 of 5 qualifying ADLs**, or
  - needs help with **2 ADLs** where **1 requires extensive assistance**, or
  - needs help with **2 ADLs** where **1 requires full dependence**; and
- **resides in** a qualifying congregate setting, including:
  - **an Adult Care Home (ACH)** licensed by North Carolina, or
  - a **combination home**, or
  - certain licensed group homes. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

The same policy says Medicaid covers specified PCS tasks in these settings, including hands-on assistance with qualifying ADLs, related cueing/prompting, certain related IADLs, medication assistance tied to the documented condition, help with adaptive devices or DME tied to the ADLs, and certain special assistance/delegated tasks. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## Important limits

Coverage is **not automatic just because someone lives in assisted living**. The beneficiary also must meet additional conditions, including that:

- the setting is licensed and verified;
- the place of service is safe;
- no other third-party payer is responsible;
- no family/household/informal caregiver is available, willing, and able to provide the authorized services at those times;
- the services are directly linked to the documented condition;
- the beneficiary is under a physician’s ongoing direct care; and
- the beneficiary is medically stable and does not require continuous licensed nursing care, monitoring, or supervision. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## Assessment / authorization requirements

A physician attestation of medical necessity is required, and new-admission PCS assessments in congregate facilities must be face-to-face in the beneficiary’s facility by an independent assessor using NC Medicaid’s standardized process. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

If by “assisted living facility” you mean a **North Carolina licensed Adult Care Home or similar qualifying congregate facility**, then **yes, NC Medicaid can cover PCS there** — **if the beneficiary meets the ADL/medical-necessity criteria and the assessment/authorization rules**. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

I checked amendments for both Policy **3L-1** and **3L**; the tool returned **3L-1** and **3L** as the authoritative current documents for this question.

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover chiropractic services under Clinical Coverage Policy 5B?
per_question.agent_answer:
No. Clinical Coverage Policy 5B does **not** cover chiropractic services as a service category. Policy 5B governs **orthotics and prosthetics** only, and its coverage criteria are limited to orthotic and prosthetic devices that meet the policy’s medical-necessity and ordering requirements. [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)]

Under Policy 5B, Medicaid covers items only when they are orthotic or prosthetic devices and, among other things:

- are ordered by a **physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner**;
- are medically necessary to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level; and
- meet the policy’s device-specific criteria. [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)]

The policy also says unlisted requests must still fit the definition of an **orthotic or prosthetic** under Policy 5B. [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)]

per_question.question: What is the treatment plan (plan of care) requirement for outpatient therapy services under NC Medicaid policy 10A?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under **NC Medicaid Clinical Coverage Policy 10A**, outpatient therapy services must have a **treatment plan (plan of care)** that includes all of the following:

- **Start date and end date**, with a duration of **no more than six months**
- **Discipline-specific treatment diagnosis** and any related medical diagnoses
- The beneficiary’s **rehabilitative or habilitative potential**
- **Defined goals** for each therapeutic discipline that are:
  - **specific and measurable**, and
  - reasonably expected to be achieved within the plan period
- The **skilled interventions, methodology, procedures, and specific programs** to be used
- The **frequency of services**
- The **length of each treatment visit in minutes**
- The **name, credentials, and signature** of the professional completing the treatment plan, **dated on or before the start date** of the plan

That is the policy’s direct plan-of-care requirement. In addition, the provider’s records must include **a copy of the treatment plan** as part of the documentation for services. per_question.question: Can a CAP/DA beneficiary transfer between service providers, and what rules govern transfers of eligible beneficiaries?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. A CAP/DA beneficiary can transfer, and the governing CAP/DA rule requires the Case Management Entity (CME) to coordinate the transfer so there are no gaps in services. The policy also preserves the beneficiary’s right to choose among Medicaid-enrolled providers. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) (effective Sept. 1, 2025), §§ 3.3, 5.4.2.

## Rules governing transfers of eligible beneficiaries

Under CAP/DA policy § 3.3, the CME must coordinate the transfer and complete these steps before the transfer:

- determine the anticipated start date of service;
- coordinate a transition plan between provider agencies;
- discuss and plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being;
- initiate transfer of the electronic health record in the CAP Business System (e-CAP/DA) to the receiving county;
- arrange a home visit within 5 business days after the beneficiary moves to the new primary residence, so the receiving entity can assess the environment for health and welfare concerns and plan mitigation; and
- coordinate services so they begin on the first date of transfer. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) § 3.3.

## If the beneficiary is transferring to a different county

Section 3.3 adds county-specific rules:

- the transferring CME designee must coordinate with the receiving CME designee on the agreed transfer date, or within less than 30 calendar days of the request to transfer;
- both agencies must plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being;
- the electronic health record must be transferred to the receiving county;
- the receiving CME designee must arrange the 5-business-day home visit after the move; and
- services must start on the first date of transfer into the receiving county. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) § 3.3.

## Beneficiary choice of provider

CAP/DA’s person-centered service plan must:

- document the authorized provider name, amount, frequency, and duration of each service; and
- ensure the beneficiary’s right to choose among providers, shown by a signed freedom-of-choice form. It also requires recognition of the beneficiary’s choice between CAP/DA, institutionalization, and among Medicaid-enrolled providers. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) § 5.4.2.

## About the federal rule cited in the frame

I could not verify that 42 CFR § 413.64 governs beneficiary transfers between CAP/DA service providers. The text retrieved for § 413.64 addresses payment rules for providers on a reasonable-cost basis, not transfer rights or transfer procedures for CAP/DA beneficiaries. [42 CFR Part 413](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-413) § 413.64.

## Bottom line

A CAP/DA beneficiary may transfer between providers or counties, but the transfer must be coordinated by the CME under CAP/DA § 3.3 to avoid any break in services and to protect health and safety. The beneficiary’s provider choice is protected by § 5.4.2 through the required freedom-of-choice documentation. Both cited documents were checked for amendments; the authoritative current CAP/DA policy is the Sept. 1, 2025 version of 3K-2, and 42 CFR Part 413 appears current in the corpus.

per_question.question: Is there a maximum earned income limit for people on HCWD (Health Coverage for Workers with Disabilities), and what premiums apply?
per_question.agent_answer:
No—NC Medicaid HCWD does **not** impose a maximum **earned** income limit that cuts off eligibility. But there **is** a cap on **unearned** income, and HCWD uses a sliding cost-sharing structure with an annual enrollment fee and, at higher income levels, monthly premiums. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf); [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)

## Income limit rule

HCWD requires the person to “meet the income requirements for his coverage group,” but the key HCWD income rule is that:

- people with **unearned income greater than 150% FPL are not eligible** for HCWD; and
- the 2014 HCWD Phase III change notice revised MA-2180 “to remove limits on countable income except for the **150% FPL cap on unearned income** and provide information about sliding scale premiums.” [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf); [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)

So, based on the policy text I retrieved, **there is no maximum earned-income ceiling for HCWD eligibility itself**. Instead, higher **total countable income** affects what the person must pay.

## What premiums and fees apply

Under MA-2180:

- If **total countable income is 150% FPL or less**: no cost sharing other than ordinary co-pays.
- If **total countable income is more than 150% FPL**: the person must pay a **$50 annual enrollment fee**.
- If **total countable monthly income exceeds 200% FPL**: the person must pay a **monthly premium in addition to the $50 annual enrollment fee**.
- Premiums rise by income range until income exceeds **450% FPL**, at which point the person owes a **full premium**. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf); [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)

## Current premium chart status

The MA-2180 premium chart has been amended, and the most recent amendment I found says: **“MA-2180.IV.I - HCWD Premiums Income chart has been updated.”** Effective date: **January 1, 2025**. [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 03-25, 2025 Federal Poverty Level Changes (FPL) Income Changes](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/CN-NO-03-25.docx.pdf)

I could verify from that 2025 change notice that the chart was updated, but the retrieved text of the notice does **not** include the actual new dollar amounts. So I can confirm the structure of premiums, but I **cannot verify the current 2025 dollar thresholds** from the text I retrieved.

## Dollar amounts shown in the MA-2180 chart I retrieved

The MA-2180 section text currently available in the corpus shows this premium schedule:

- **0–150% FPL**: $0 premium  
- **151–200% FPL**: $0 premium  
- **201–250% FPL**: **$196 individual / $265 couple**
- **251–300% FPL**: **$235 individual / $318 couple**
- **301–350% FPL**: **$274 individual / $370 couple**
- **351–400% FPL**: **$313 individual / $423 couple**
- **401–450% FPL**: **$352 individual / $476 couple**
- **451% FPL and above**: **$875** [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)

Because MA-2180’s premium chart was updated by the **2025 FPL change notice**, I would treat those **premium amounts** as potentially superseded for current use unless you have the updated chart.

## Bottom line

- **Maximum earned income limit?** **No**, not as a hard eligibility cutoff in the HCWD policy text I found.
- **Important limit?** Yes: **unearned income over 150% FPL makes the person ineligible**.
- **Premiums/fees?**
  - up to **150% FPL**: no premium;
  - over **150% FPL**: **$50 annual enrollment fee**;
  - over **200% FPL**: monthly premium plus the annual fee;
  - over **450% FPL**: full premium. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf); [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf); [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 03-25, 2025 Federal Poverty Level Changes (FPL) Income Changes](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/CN-NO-03-25.docx.pdf)

If you want, I can next help you translate this into a practical rule like: “If my client earns $X/month and has $Y unearned income, what HCWD fee/premium bucket are they in?”

per_question.question: How many days of therapeutic leave from a nursing facility does NC Medicaid allow per year, and what conditions must be met?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid allows **up to 60 days of therapeutic leave per calendar year** from a nursing facility bed.

## Conditions that must be met

- Therapeutic leave does **not apply** if the resident is absent **to receive inpatient or nursing services paid by Medicaid** elsewhere, or at a different level of care in the same facility.

per_question.question: If a Private Duty Nursing provider terminates services for a Medicaid beneficiary, what notification requirements must they follow?
per_question.agent_answer:
A PDN provider that discharges a Medicaid beneficiary must notify **NC Medicaid within 5 business days**, and the exact submission depends on why services are ending.

## NC Medicaid PDN policy requirements

Under **Section 5.2.4.1, “Notification of Termination,”** of **[3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)**, which appears current based on the amendment record I checked:

- **If the PDN provider discharges the beneficiary:**  
  The provider must submit the **DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form)** to NC Medicaid **within five (5) business days**.

- **If the provider discharges the beneficiary because another source of nursing care coverage is available:**  
  The provider must, within **five (5) business days**:
  - **notify NC Medicaid**, and
  - submit the **DMA-3513**.  
  That notification must include:
  - the **last date PDN services were provided and may be billed to Medicaid**, and
  - the **name of the other source of coverage**.

- **If the attending physician discharges the beneficiary:**  
  The PDN provider must provide NC Medicaid, within **five (5) business days**:
  - the **attending physician’s order terminating PDN services**, and
  - the **DMA-3513**.

- **If services end because the beneficiary loses NC Medicaid eligibility, or no PDN services are provided for 30 consecutive days** for any reason, including hospitalization:  
  The policy says the **prior approval process must be initiated again** under Sections 5.1 and 5.2 before services resume. It does not add a separate provider notice requirement in that sentence beyond the termination rules above. [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment), § 5.2.4.1.

## What about notice to the beneficiary?

The PDN policy section I retrieved does **not** say the provider must give the beneficiary a separate advance written termination notice when the **provider or physician** discharges the beneficiary. In fact, it says:  
> “The decision of the beneficiary’s attending physician and/or the PDN service provider to discharge the beneficiary cannot be appealed to NC Medicaid.”  
[3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment), § 5.2.4.1.

By contrast, if **NC Medicaid** terminates PDN because eligibility, policy criteria, or medical necessity is not met, then **NC Medicaid or its designee** must provide the beneficiary/legal representative **written notice of an adverse decision including appeal rights**. That same 3G-1 section states this directly. And in managed care, federal rules require written notice of an adverse benefit determination that is timely, adequate, and consistent with accessibility/language standards. See [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), §§ 438.404, 438.10.

## Bottom line

For a **provider-initiated PDN termination**, the clearest NC Medicaid requirement I could verify is:

- **Submit DMA-3513 to NC Medicaid within 5 business days**; and
- if termination is due to **other nursing coverage**, also notify Medicaid of the **last billable date** and the **other coverage source**; and
- if termination is ordered by the **attending physician**, send the **physician’s termination order plus DMA-3513** within **5 business days**.

per_question.question: What does federal law define as 'home health services' under Medicaid, and where must they be provided?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal Medicaid law, **“home health services”** are the services listed in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(b)** when they are provided to a beneficiary **at the beneficiary’s place of residence** and under the required practitioner orders and plan-of-care rules. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## What counts as “home health services”
Under **42 C.F.R. § 440.70**, home health services include:

- **Nursing services** provided on a part-time or intermittent basis
- **Home health aide services**
- **Medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** suitable for use in settings where normal life activities take place
- **Physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech pathology and audiology services**  
  - The first three categories are required home health services under the regulation, and therapy services are optional for states. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

The regulation also says coverage of home health services **cannot be conditioned on the beneficiary needing nursing or therapy services**. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Required ordering and plan-of-care rules
Federal law requires that home health services be provided:

- On **orders written by a physician, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant**, working in accordance with state law, for the services described in § 440.70(b)(1), (2), and (4)
- As part of a **written plan of care**
- With the ordering practitioner reviewing that plan of care **every 60 days** for those services

For medical supplies, equipment, and appliances under **§ 440.70(b)(3)**, the regulation uses a slightly different ordering rule:
- They must be provided on a physician’s order or the order of another **licensed practitioner of the healing arts** acting within state-law scope of practice
- Under a **written plan of care**
- With review as specified in the regulation, including at least **annual review of the beneficiary’s need** and further review frequency determined case by case based on the nature of the item. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Where they must be provided
Federal law says home health services must be provided **at the beneficiary’s place of residence**. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

But the regulation also defines what **does not** count as a “place of residence” for this purpose. It excludes:

- a **hospital**
- a **nursing facility**
- an **intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ICF/IID)**, except for certain home health services in an ICF/IID that the facility itself is not required to provide. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

The rule further clarifies that a beneficiary may receive home health services in **“any setting in which normal life activities take place,”** other than:
- a hospital
- a nursing facility
- an ICF/IID
- or **any setting where Medicaid payment is or could be made for inpatient services that include room and board**. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

And importantly, federal law says **home health services cannot be limited to beneficiaries who are homebound**. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Bottom line
Federal Medicaid law defines home health services as the covered nursing, aide, medical-supply/equipment/appliance, and certain therapy services listed in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(b)**, provided under the required orders and written plan of care. They must be furnished **at the beneficiary’s place of residence**, meaning generally a setting where normal life activities occur, **not** a hospital, nursing facility, or most ICF/IID placements. The cited federal authority appears current, and I did not find any separate amendment notice in this corpus displacing **42 CFR Part 440** as the authoritative source. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

per_question.question: How does NC Medicaid define 'terminally ill' for purposes of hospice eligibility, and what certification is required?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid hospice, a beneficiary is treated as **“terminally ill”** when the hospice certification supports a **life expectancy of six months or less** if the illness runs its normal course. The policy’s certification/recertification requirements repeatedly use that six-month standard as the basis for hospice eligibility and continued eligibility. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) (effective Mar. 15, 2024), § 5.4.1; Attachment B, “D. Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness.”

## Required certification

NC Medicaid requires **written certification of terminal illness for each benefit period**. The hospice provider must obtain the written certification **before submitting a claim for payment**. If the written certification cannot be obtained within **two calendar days after a period begins**, an **oral certification** must be obtained within those two days, and the written certification still must be completed before the claim is submitted. Certifications may be completed no more than **15 calendar days before** the effective date of election, and recertifications no more than **15 calendar days before** the start of the next benefit period. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.1.

## Who must sign it

For the **initial 90-day period**, the hospice must obtain a written certification from:

- **the hospice medical director or the physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group (IDG)**; and
- **the individual’s attending physician**, if the individual has one.

For **subsequent benefit periods**, only the **hospice medical director or physician member of the IDG** must certify. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.3.

## What the certification must contain

The certification or recertification must include:

- a physician narrative that **briefly synthesizes the clinical information supporting the terminal diagnosis**;
- the physician’s attestation that the narrative was composed **after reviewing the clinical information** and, when applicable, **examining the beneficiary**;
- a narrative that reflects the beneficiary’s **individual clinical circumstances**;
- the **election period dates** to which the certification applies; and
- the certifying or recertifying physician’s **signature and date**.

For the **third and later election periods**, the narrative must also explain why the findings from the required face-to-face encounter support a **life expectancy of six months or less**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), Attachment B, “D. Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness.”

## Additional recertification requirement

Before the **third benefit period recertification** and every recertification after that, a **hospice physician or hospice nurse practitioner** must have a **face-to-face encounter** with the beneficiary, occurring no more than **30 calendar days before** that recertification, to gather clinical findings for continued eligibility. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.1.

I checked amendments for Clinical Coverage Policy 3D and the tool returned the current authoritative document as **Hospice Services**, effective **March 15, 2024**, with no listed amendments in the corpus.

per_question.question: What ambulance services are NOT covered by NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid does **not** cover ambulance services that fall outside the policy’s covered criteria, and it specifically lists several non-covered situations and charges.

## Not covered

Under the current **Ambulance Services** policy, the following are **not covered**:

- **An ambulance is called and no treatment is needed**
- **The ambulance responds to a false alarm**
- **The beneficiary refuses all medical services**
- **Ambulance transport for a medical service that is not itself covered by Medicaid**
- **Commercial airline tickets**
- **Airstrip fees**
- **Taxes** charged separately (local, state, federal, etc.)
- **Separate additional charges for nursing personnel** who are employees of a facility or ambulance service
- **Waiting fees**
- **Separate charges for oxygen and other items/supplies**, because those are included in the base rate and are not separately reimbursable
- **Any ambulance services other than those listed in Section 3.2 as covered services** [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)

## Other important limitations

NC Medicaid also states that:

- **Loaded mileage to a facility that is not the nearest appropriate facility is not reimbursed**
- A hospital is not considered “appropriate” just because a physician has staff privileges there
- A beneficiary’s personal preference does not determine whether a facility is appropriate [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)

## General non-coverage rules

Ambulance services are also not covered if:

- the beneficiary does not meet eligibility requirements in Section 2.0;
- the beneficiary does not meet the coverage criteria in Section 3.0;
- the service duplicates another provider’s service; or
- the service is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)

## Coverage rule this contrasts with

The policy’s covered rule says Medicaid covers **emergency services** needed to **screen and stabilize** the beneficiary, without prior authorization when a prudent layperson would reasonably believe an emergency medical condition exists. So if the ambulance service does not fit the covered criteria in Section 3.2, it is not covered [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)

**Current source:** Clinical Coverage Policy **15, Ambulance Services**, effective **December 15, 2023**. I checked for amendments and the policy document itself is the current authoritative source.

per_question.question: Are there quantity limits on prescription drugs under NC Medicaid, and when is prior authorization required for pharmacy claims?

- **Prior authorization is required** when a drug is on NC Medicaid’s pharmacy prior-approval list or otherwise meets NC Medicaid PA criteria.
- A claim can also reject because **PA limits are exceeded**, which is distinct from the general fact that some drugs require PA. [[Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)]

Policy 9 identifies a specific set of drugs and drug classes under **“Pharmacy Prior Approval Drugs and Criteria.”** That list includes, for example, categories such as:

- GLP-1 receptor agonists and combinations
- Hepatitis C medications
- Growth hormones
- Opioid analgesics
- Triptans
- Certain behavioral health clinical edits
- and many other named drugs/classes in the policy’s PA criteria list. [[Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)]

Policy 9 also states in its **Requirements for and Limitations on Coverage** that PA applies to items such as:

- new variations of products already in the marketplace,
- new indications for existing products,
- changes in indications, and
- changes in dosing for products already in the marketplace. [[Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)]

If a request seeks an **exception** to FDA-approved guidelines, evidence-based standards, or NC Medicaid drug criteria, the prescriber must support it with documentation such as:

- health record information showing medical necessity,
- explanation of what other drugs were tried or cannot be tried,
- explanation why standard FDA or NC Medicaid criteria are insufficient for the beneficiary, and
- supporting compendia or peer-reviewed literature. Policy 9 § 3.2.3. [[Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)]

The policy materials retrieved support that NC Medicaid uses claim edits and limitations in pharmacy processing, including denials/messages tied to limits. PA LIMITS EXCEEDED.”** [[Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)]

So the safest answer is:

1. **Yes, NC Medicaid imposes quantity-related limits for some drugs/claims.**
2. **Prior authorization is required when the drug or claim falls within NC Medicaid’s listed PA drug categories or criteria.**

per_question.question: Under what conditions can speech therapy be provided via telehealth under NC Medicaid?

Yes—NC Medicaid allows some speech-language services by telehealth, but only under specific conditions.

## Telehealth conditions for speech therapy

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A**, a **select set of speech and language evaluation and treatment interventions** may be delivered by telehealth. Telehealth is permitted when it is **medically necessary**, including when:

- the beneficiary’s medical condition is such that **exposure to others should be avoided**, or
- the beneficiary is in a **remote or underserved location** where access to appropriately qualified providers is limited.  
  [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2/1/2025, sec. “e. Telehealth”]

NC Medicaid also imposes these beneficiary-specific limits:

- **Telehealth must be an adjunct to in-person care, not a replacement**, unless in-person care is **contraindicated or unavailable**.
- It must be used **in the beneficiary’s best interest**, **not for therapist convenience**.
- It **cannot be used solely to increase therapist productivity**.  
  [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2/1/2025, sec. “e. Telehealth”]

## Which speech-language services are telehealth-eligible

Policy 10A identifies specific speech/language evaluation and treatment codes that are telehealth-eligible.

### Telehealth-eligible speech/language evaluation services
- **92521** — Yes
- **92522** — Yes
- **92523** — Yes
- **92524** — Yes
- **92607** — Yes
- **92608** — Yes

Not telehealth-eligible in that table:
- **92551**
- **92610**

### Telehealth-eligible speech/language treatment services

## Ordinary medical-necessity rules still apply

Telehealth availability does **not** remove the normal coverage requirements for speech-language therapy. For example, Policy 10A’s speech-language therapy section still requires medically necessary treatment and documentation for covered services, including specific documented findings for dysphagia-related treatment.  
[[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2/1/2025, sec. 3.2.1.3]

## Bottom line

Speech therapy can be provided via telehealth under NC Medicaid **only for the speech/language services that Policy 10A marks as telehealth-eligible**, and only when telehealth is **medically necessary**, used **in the beneficiary’s best interest**, and generally **supplements rather than replaces in-person care** unless in-person care is contraindicated or unavailable.

per_question.question: What medical loss ratio (MLR) must Medicaid managed care organizations meet under federal law, and how does NC implement this requirement?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal Medicaid managed care rules, plans do **not automatically have to meet a universal minimum MLR**. What federal law requires in all cases is that the state ensure each Medicaid MCO, PIHP, and PAHP **calculates and reports** an MLR. If a state **chooses** to impose a minimum MLR, that minimum must be **at least 85%**. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

## Federal rule

### 1) What is always required
Federal law says the state must ensure, through its contracts, that each Medicaid managed care organization calculates and reports an MLR in accordance with the regulation. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8(a)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

### 2) What the minimum threshold is, if the state adopts one
The federal regulation does **not itself impose an across-the-board mandatory 85% minimum** on every Medicaid managed care plan. Instead, it says:

- **If a state elects to mandate a minimum MLR**, that minimum must be **equal to or higher than 85%**; and
- the MLR must be calculated and reported for each reporting year. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8(c)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

So the short answer is: **85% is the federal floor for any state-imposed minimum MLR**, not an unconditional federal minimum applicable in every state.

### 3) Federal oversight if a state uses a minimum MLR
If a state requires remittances when a plan misses the state’s minimum MLR, the state must:

- annually submit to CMS a summary of each plan’s MLR report, including the numerator, denominator, MLR percentage, member months, and any remittances owed; and
- reimburse CMS for the federal share of any remittance and submit a separate methodology report on that calculation. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.74](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

## How North Carolina implements it

Based on the NC material retrieved here, North Carolina implements the federal framework by **assuring CMS that, if an MCO/PIHP/PAHP owes a remittance for failing to meet the state-required minimum MLR, NC will**:

- reimburse CMS for the federal share of that remittance, taking account of matching-rate differences; and
- submit a separate report describing the methodology used to determine the state and federal shares, along with the annual report summarizing plan MLR reports. [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care, § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment)

The NC SPA text also states that the state assures its rates are designed to reasonably achieve a medical loss ratio, but the excerpt retrieved here is truncated and **does not clearly state in the text provided what specific minimum percentage NC contractually requires**. So from the materials I reviewed, I can verify NC’s **reporting/remittance implementation**, but I **could not verify from the retrieved NC section alone** whether NC expressly sets a specific contractual MLR percentage beyond the federal rule that any state-imposed minimum must be at least 85%. [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care, § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

- **Federal law:** plans must **calculate and report** MLR; if a state imposes a minimum, it must be **at least 85%**. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)
- **NC implementation shown here:** NC assures CMS it will handle **annual reporting and remittances** consistent with the federal MLR oversight rules. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.74](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438); [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care, § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment)

per_question.question: What are the specific criteria for NC Medicaid coverage of CAR-T cell therapy?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid covers CAR-T cell therapy only if the beneficiary meets the policy’s general coverage rules **and** the therapy meets the policy’s CAR-T-specific requirements. Under the current **Clinical Coverage Policy 11A-17**, the specific CAR-T criteria are:

## Specific coverage criteria for CAR-T therapy

1. **The CAR-T product must have FDA approval.**
2. **It must be administered according to the FDA-approved guidelines**, including:
   - indications and usage,
   - dosage and administration,
   - dosage forms and strengths, and
   - warnings and precautions.
3. **It must be given at a certified or authorized treatment center.**
4. **If the CAR-T therapy is subject to an FDA-required REMS program**, the treatment center must be enrolled in that REMS, and providers must be trained to manage:
   - cytokine release syndrome (CRS), and
   - neurologic toxicities.  
   [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), §§ 3.2, 3.2.1, effective 4/1/2025.

## General coverage criteria that also must be met

In addition to the CAR-T-specific rules, NC Medicaid requires that the service be:

- individualized, specific, and consistent with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis;
- safely furnished, with no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide; and
- provided in a manner not primarily for the convenience of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 3.1, effective 4/1/2025.

## When NC Medicaid specifically will not cover it

The same policy says CAR-T is not covered if, among other things:

- the product is **not FDA-approved**;
- it is administered **outside FDA guidelines** for indications/usage, dosage/administration, or dosage forms/strengths;
- a therapy requiring REMS is administered at a facility **not enrolled** in that REMS;
- it is a **repeat treatment** for a beneficiary who previously received another CAR-T therapy;
- the beneficiary’s psychosocial history limits ability to comply with pre- and post-infusion care; or
- current beneficiary or caretaker noncompliance makes adherence to the required medical regimen improbable.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), §§ 4.1, 4.2.1, effective 4/1/2025.

## Prior approval documentation typically required

For prior approval, NC Medicaid also requires documentation such as:

- a physician-signed letter of medical necessity,
- past chemotherapy regimens and dates,
- clinical and social history,
- verification that the administering facility is qualified/authorized for that CAR-T product,
- recent HIV and hepatitis serologies,
- diagnostic and procedure results including bone marrow biopsy,
- and a psychological/social evaluation addressing compliance, support network, post-treatment care plan, and relevant mental health, substance use, or legal history.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 5.2.2, effective 4/1/2025.

I checked amendments for Policy 11A-17, and the authoritative current document is the **4/1/2025** version of **Clinical Coverage Policy 11A-17, CAR-T Cell Therapy**.

per_question.question: Can an NC Innovations waiver participant request services that exceed their individual base budget, and what happens if they believe their needs cannot be met within the budget?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. An NC Innovations participant may request services that cost more than the participant’s individual base budget, and the base budget is not a binding cap.

## Short answer

If the participant believes their needs cannot be met within the base budget, they can request additional services. Under NC Innovations, the SIS results and base budget are “guidelines” only, and if the LME/MCO finds the services medically necessary, the services “will be authorized, regardless of the base budget.” If the request is denied, the participant must be told the reasons and how to appeal, and the policy also references how to file a grievance about the base budget. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (effective 2016-11-01, current; section titled “Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes”).

## What the governing rules say

### 1) Federal HCBS waiver rules
Federal HCBS waiver rules require a person-centered service plan and contemplate that the waiver will specify whether the state may refuse services when expected waiver costs exceed the cost of an equivalent institutional level of care. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301(a)(3), (b)(1), (c) (current).

That means the relevant upper-level constraint is the waiver structure and medical-necessity / level-of-care framework, not the participant’s individual base budget by itself.

### 2) NC Innovations policy
NC Innovations states:

- the participant “may request services that cost in excess of his or her base budget if he or she believes his or her needs cannot be met within his or her base budget”;
- “the results of the SIS and the base budget are guidelines that do not constitute a binding limit on the amount of services that may be requested or authorized”; and
- “if the LME/MCO determines services to be medically necessary, they will be authorized, regardless of the base budget.” [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (effective 2016-11-01, current; “Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes”).

## What happens if the participant says the budget is not enough

If the participant believes the base budget will not meet their needs:

- they can ask for services above the base budget;
- the LME/MCO must evaluate whether those services are medically necessary; and
- if approved as medically necessary, the services are authorized even though they exceed the budget. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment).

If the request is denied:

- the LME/MCO must notify the participant of the reasons for the denial and how to appeal; and
- the participant may also file a grievance regarding the base budget. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment).

## Related detail on high-intensity service requests

The policy also shows that unusually high service levels can still be authorized, with added review:

- up to 12 hours/day may be authorized for the full plan year;
- up to 16 hours/day may be authorized for a six-month period within the plan year;
- more than 16 hours/day may be authorized for up to 90 days, and extensions beyond that require review of medical necessity.  
The treatment team should then review the person’s status and identify sustainable supports, including options inside and outside the waiver, such as Medicaid State Plan services. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (effective 2016-11-01, current).

## One caution

I did not find language in the retrieved sections saying that every request above base budget must be approved. The policy says approval turns on medical necessity and the LME/MCO’s determination. So the strongest supported statement is:

> A participant can request services above the base budget, and the base budget alone cannot be treated as an absolute cap; but authorization still depends on a medical-necessity determination under the waiver.

## Income/payment point

Federal HCBS rules also provide that for certain waiver participants, Medicaid’s payment for HCBS may be reduced by the participant’s post-eligibility income contribution after required deductions. That rule affects payment treatment, not whether the participant may request services above the base budget. [42 CFR Part 435](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-435) § 435.726 (current).
